title: Luke (18 October)
hook: the physician evangelist, patron of doctors and artists

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hedwig, the duchess who gave her wealth away to the poor. Your line was the duchess who gave.

Near the end of the letter to the Colossians, Paul passes on greetings from the people around him. Some get a name and little more. One gets a name and a job: "Luke the most dear physician." A companion of Paul, a doctor, someone Paul was glad to have nearby. His name turns up a few times in Paul's letters, always briefly. And yet the Church's tradition puts his name on a whole Gospel and on the Acts of the Apostles. Doctors keep him as their patron. So do painters.
screen: `A GREETING AT THE END OF A LETTER.` → `LUKE THE MOST DEAR PHYSICIAN.` → `DOCTORS AND PAINTERS CLAIM HIM.`

segments.voice: His Gospel opens not with an angel or a manger, but with one reader, a man named Theophilus. Others, the writer says, have set out to tell these things. He has looked into all of it carefully from the start, and now he'll write it down in order, so Theophilus can be sure of what he was taught. That's someone who checks. The Acts of the Apostles speaks to the same Theophilus, which is why tradition reads the two books as one work in two parts, by one hand. Then the doctor's eye. Luke's Gospel is where you meet the good Samaritan bending over a beaten man on the road, pouring in oil and wine and binding up his wounds. It's where the prodigal son comes home hungry and the father runs. It's full of people at the edges: the sick, the poor, widows, outsiders. Some readers hear a physician in that, someone used to sitting with people in their worst week. Now the painters. Tradition says Luke painted Mary, and some old icons of her have been called his. Nobody can prove a brush was ever in his hand. But his first chapters are where Mary stands in full: the angel's greeting, the visit to Elizabeth, the birth, the shepherds. And then one quiet line: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Whether or not he painted her, he gave artists their scenes.
screen: `WRITTEN IN ORDER, FOR THEOPHILUS.` · `ONE WORK IN TWO PARTS.` · `A DOCTOR'S EYE FOR THE WOUNDED.` · `HE GAVE PAINTERS THEIR SCENES.` · then, large: `MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Find a pen and the back of an envelope, and draw one thing in front of you, a cup, your own hand, a window, looking at it more than at the page. It doesn't need to be good; the point is to look at one thing long enough to see it, the way a doctor looks at a patient, the way Luke's pages linger on Mary. If you pray, offer the looking itself as a prayer; if not, just keep your eyes and your hand moving together.
Luke. A companion of Paul, called the most dear physician, whom tradition names as the writer of a Gospel and of Acts, and the patron of doctors and artists.
Your line: the physician. Unhurried, close and kind: that's a doctor's kind of attention. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Luke on 18 October; doctors, nurses and artists often ask his prayers, and some hospitals and medical guilds bear his name.

chat.says: Who was Luke, anyway? Just a name on one of the Gospels?
options: Paul's dear physician; tradition says he wrote a Gospel and Acts for Theophilus.
One of the twelve, a fisherman Jesus called away from his nets in Galilee.
A later monk who collected other people's stories without checking any of them.
